articleText: India’s tiger population has rebounded to about 3,682, yet 30-35% now live outside protected areas, raising human-tiger conflicts. In Karnataka’s Badagalapura village, farmer Mahadeva Gowda was mauled by a tiger in October 2025, leaving him permanently blind; a second farmer, Rajashekarappa, was killed two weeks later. The Karnataka Forest Department has captured 30 tigers between September 2025 and May 2026, releasing all but two—one to a zoo, one to a rehabilitation centre. Similar captures occur near Bandhavgarh, Tadoba-Andhari, and other reserves. Experts say tigers disperse for territory or because they cannot hunt effectively, and that relocation often merely shifts the problem to another area. The National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) now promotes landscape-scale management, corridor restoration, and monitoring of tigers outside reserves, aiming to balance tiger conservation with human safety. The challenge is to manage shared landscapes, maintain ecological connectivity, and reduce conflict while sustaining tiger numbers.
